note: Why a blues in A has three dominant 7th chords: their roots ringed on a staff and the chords counted the long way, the three chord boxes heard, then A7's own notes on an arpeggio-neck with its 3rd and ♭7 ringed and named. The why is the mechanism (only the 5th chord is a dominant 7th in a major key; the blues makes all three one), and the key stays A, since the note names are the lesson.

exercise.title: Why the blues uses three 7th chords
exercise.why: In a major key only the 5th chord is a dominant 7th, but in a blues all three chords are, so every chord carries a ♭7 that leans away and the music never quite settles.

cells.text: {{chord:I7}} is the 1st chord of the blues in A, built on {{1}}. {{chord:IV7}} is the 4th chord, built on {{4}}, and {{chord:V7}} is the 5th chord, built on {{5}}. Tap the three ringed notes on the staff below to hear them.

Press each chord box below to hear the three chords.
Listen for the same dominant 7th sound three times, built on three different roots.

The neck below shows the notes of {{chord:I7}}. Tap them from the lowest note to the highest and back.
The ringed {{3}} is {{c-sharp}} and the ringed {{b7}} is {{g}}. {{g}} is in the A minor pentatonic scale and {{c-sharp}} is not, so over this chord a blues solo often slides from {{c}} up to {{c-sharp}}.
Practice until you can find the ringed {{3}} without looking for it.
